question: What is the Bayesian optimal regret of k-armed bandits, and when can the Bayesian optimal policy be computed tractably (one-armed finite horizon, Gittins index for discounted infinite horizon)?
contributions: Bounds on Bayesian optimal regret from frequentist bounds
Exact DP for Bernoulli and approximate DP for Gaussian one-armed bandits
Gittins index theorem with full proof, and Varaiya's algorithm

results.claim: Bayesian optimal regret is at most the minimax regret, so BR*_n(Q) <= C sqrt(kn); and a prior exists attaining c sqrt(kn), so sup_Q BR*_n(Q) = Theta(sqrt(kn)).
results.setup: Bayesian bandits (Bernoulli, k arms, prior Q on [0,1]^k); Bayesian optimal regret BR*_n(Q); universal constants C,c

results.claim: For any fixed prior Q, BR*_n(Q)/n^(1/2) tends to 0 (limsup), but some prior has liminf BR*_n/n^(1/2-eps) = infinity for all eps>0 (Theorem 35.1).
results.setup: Bayesian bandits (Bernoulli, k arms, prior Q on [0,1]^k); Bayesian optimal regret BR*_n(Q); proof left as Exercise 35.1

results.claim: For regular priors the Bayesian optimal regret is Theta(log^2 n); Lai (1987) gives BR*_n ~ c log(n)^2.
results.setup: sufficiently regular priors and noise models

results.claim: The pathological prior for the sqrt(n)-ish lower bound puts mass at least c/log(1/Delta) on bandits with min gap <= Delta.
Backwards induction for the Bernoulli one-armed Bayesian bandit costs O(n^2), versus O(n) for a typical frequentist stopping rule.
results.setup: One Bernoulli arm with Beta(alpha,beta) prior, known arm mu2, horizon n; states s in {0..t} per round
results.quote: The total computation for this backwards induction is O(n2), and the output

results.claim: Experiment 35.1 setup: horizon n=500, mu2=1/2, Beta(1,1) prior; Bayesian optimal policy vs the frequentist stopping rule (35.4).
results.setup: Bernoulli one-armed bandit, expected regret vs mu1; Fig 35.2 axes show regret 0-8
results.note: Regret values are only in Fig 35.2 (not tabulated); axis ticks 0..8 read from the figure.
results.quote: The horizon is set to n = 500 and µ2 = 1/2.

results.claim: In Experiment 35.1 the frequentist rule has very small regret for mu1>1/2 but large regret for mu1<1/2 because its conservative confidence interval makes it stop later; averaged over the prior it loses to the Bayesian optimal policy.
results.setup: n=500, mu2=1/2, uniform prior on mu1

results.claim: Gaussian one-armed case: the value function w_t is increasing, convex, with w_t(mu)/mu -> n-t+1 as mu->inf and w_t -> (n-t+1)mu2 as mu->-inf (Lemma 35.5); approximated by piecewise quadratics in O(Nn) time for N knots.
results.setup: N(nu,1) arm, N(mu_P,sigma_P^2) prior, known arm mu2
results.quote: The computation time for calculating the coeﬃcients ai, bi, ci for all t and i ∈[N] is O(Nn).

results.claim: Gittins index (fair charge) is g(x)=inf{gamma: v_gamma(x)=0}, equivalently the sup over stopping times tau>=2 of expected discounted reward over expected discounted time.
results.setup: Discounted retirement game, discount alpha in (0,1)

results.claim: Gittins index theorem: the policy playing argmax_i g(S_i(t)) maximises expected total discounted reward over all policies (Theorem 35.9), for independent arms and geometric discounting.
results.setup: k independent Markov chains with common kernel, Assumption 35.6, prior factorises over arms

results.claim: Theorem 35.9 fails for non-geometric discounting and for multiple-play; the optimal finite-horizon policy is generally not an index policy.
results.setup: alpha(t) not exponential; Berry & Fristedt 1985; Pandelis & Teneketzis 1999

results.claim: Varaiya's algorithm computes all Gittins indices of a finite chain in O(|S|^4) with Gauss-Jordan, or O(|S|^(3+eps)), eps<=0.373, with faster inversion.
results.setup: finite state space S, transition matrix P, rewards r in [0,1]^|S|
results.quote: complexity of this algorithm is O(|S|4).

results.claim: Exact finite-horizon Bayesian optimal DP is feasible for small problems: n=50, k=5, Bernoulli with Beta prior has about 10^11 states.
results.setup: n=50, k=5, Bernoulli noise, Beta prior

results.claim: Undiscounted Gittins index g_n(s)=sup_{2<=tau<=n} E_s[sum r]/E_s[tau-1]; as a heuristic for k arms it is not Bayesian optimal but performs well and in the Gaussian case has UCB-like frequentist regret (Lattimore 2016a); asymptotically it behaves like the KL-UCB index (Burnetas & Katehakis 1997b).

limits: Computing the Bayesian optimal policy for finite-horizon k-armed bandits is intractable in general; no computational lower bound is known (Note 2).
Gittins theorem needs geometric discounting, independent arms with a factorised prior, single play (Note 6).
Bayesian policies are brittle when the prior is wrong (Note 1).
Gittins asymptotic result (Burnetas & Katehakis) does not give regret guarantees (Note 8).
Experiment 35.1 is a single configuration (n=500, mu2=1/2); the numeric regrets appear only in Fig 35.2.
Theorem 35.1 and several lemmas are left as exercises.
practices: Use a retirement policy for the one-armed Bayesian bandit and solve by backwards induction on sufficient statistics (p.444-445).
Use a piecewise-quadratic approximation of the value function for Gaussian one-armed bandits (p.447).
Use the Gittins index policy for discounted Bayesian bandits with factorised priors (Thm 35.9).
Compute Gittins indices for finite chains with Varaiya's algorithm; truncate the horizon when alpha is small (p.454).
For small horizons, exact DP may be worth running for mission-critical use (Note 9, p.456).
Undiscounted Gittins index of horizon n-t+1 is a good heuristic for k arms (Note 7).
